single-responsibility.name: Single Responsibility Principle
single-responsibility.summary: Separate responsibilities driven by different reasons to change.
single-responsibility.question: Why does changing an invoice layout touch its calculation?
single-responsibility.scenario: Invoice calculates totals, formats the document, and saves it. Accounting rules, presentation requests, and storage changes all modify the same class.
single-responsibility.meaning: Responsibility is about reasons to change, not the number of methods. Separate behavior driven by different stakeholders while keeping behavior that changes together close together.
single-responsibility.why: Calculations become independently testable. Changing the template or storage no longer requires editing pricing logic, and ownership becomes clearer.
single-responsibility.beforeNote: Three independent reasons to change share one class.
single-responsibility.afterNote: Calculation, presentation, and storage are separate. Their composition remains simple without a framework.
single-responsibility.when: A module repeatedly changes for unrelated business requests, or testing one behavior requires unrelated dependencies.
single-responsibility.caution: This does not mean one method per class or one line per file. Behavior that changes together usually belongs together.
single-responsibility.remember: Separate reasons to change, not lines of code.
single-responsibility.connection: Strategy can isolate replaceable algorithms; Facade can separate orchestration from subsystem responsibilities. Neither is mandatory for establishing a good boundary.

open-closed.name: Open-Closed Principle
open-closed.summary: Add behavior through extension points while keeping stable logic intact.
open-closed.question: Does adding points payment require rewriting checkout?
open-closed.scenario: Each payment method adds another branch to pay. Payment options change, but the otherwise stable checkout flow must change with them.
open-closed.meaning: Make identified variations extensible so new behavior can connect without repeatedly editing stable modules. Extension points should follow evidence of change.
open-closed.why: New payment behavior can be developed and tested independently, reducing the impact on existing flows.
open-closed.beforeNote: A new payment option requires editing the branches inside pay.
open-closed.afterNote: pay accepts one contract. A new function adds a payment behavior without changing the stable flow.
open-closed.when: The same variation keeps recurring, such as payment methods, export formats, pricing algorithms, or event handlers.
open-closed.caution: It does not forbid editing code. Bugs, flawed abstractions, and assembly configuration still need changes. Do not anticipate every imaginary variation.
open-closed.remember: Make recurring variation extensible; protect stable flows.
open-closed.connection: Strategy replaces an algorithm, Decorator adds wrapping behavior, and Observer adds subscribers. Each provides a different kind of extension point.

liskov-substitution.name: Liskov Substitution Principle
liskov-substitution.summary: Replacement implementations must preserve the promised behavior.
liskov-substitution.question: Why does a type-compatible replacement break the caller?
liskov-substitution.scenario: A caller expects a readable and writable Store. ReadOnlyStore implements that interface but throws whenever write is called, breaking the caller's expectation.
liskov-substitution.meaning: A subtype must preserve the properties callers rely on when used in place of its supertype. Matching signatures is insufficient: do not strengthen preconditions or weaken promised results.
liskov-substitution.why: Callers can use a contract without checking every concrete type. Behavioral contract tests make substitutions more trustworthy.
liskov-substitution.beforeNote: A read-only implementation claims it can write but rejects that promise.
liskov-substitution.afterNote: The read-only implementation promises Reader only. Implementations that can actually write may also promise Writer.
liskov-substitution.when: Inheritance, multiple interface implementations, plugins, or test doubles must be interchangeable.
liskov-substitution.caution: Not every exception violates the principle. Check what the shared contract permits. Type compatibility does not replace behavioral tests.
liskov-substitution.remember: Substitute behavioral promises, not just method signatures.
liskov-substitution.connection: Strategy and Proxy both need a shared behavioral contract. A proxy's access checks, results, and exceptions must conform to the contract callers were given.

interface-segregation.name: Interface Segregation Principle
interface-segregation.summary: Clients depend only on the capabilities they actually need.
interface-segregation.question: Why must a basic printer implement scanning and fax?
interface-segregation.scenario: Device bundles printing, scanning, and faxing. A basic printer must implement unsupported operations, making its actual capabilities unclear.
interface-segregation.meaning: Organize interfaces around coherent client needs. Clients should not depend on methods they do not use. One object can implement several focused interfaces.
interface-segregation.why: Dependencies become explicit, unrelated capability changes have less impact, and partial implementations need fewer placeholder methods.
interface-segregation.beforeNote: BasicPrinter satisfies the oversized interface with unsupported-operation errors.
interface-segregation.afterNote: The printing client requires Printer only. A multifunction device can implement Printer and Scanner.
interface-segregation.when: An interface keeps growing, implementations contain empty methods, or different clients use small, distinct subsets.
interface-segregation.caution: Smaller is not always better. Group a meaningful capability instead of creating an interface per method without a real consumer.
interface-segregation.remember: Shape an interface around its user's needs.
interface-segregation.connection: Adapter can expose the focused interface a client expects. Bridge can define distinct capability contracts for its two sides.

dependency-inversion.name: Dependency Inversion Principle
dependency-inversion.summary: Business policy depends on capability contracts, not technical details.
dependency-inversion.question: Why does changing notification channels modify order logic?
dependency-inversion.scenario: OrderService creates EmailSender internally. Switching to SMS or a test double requires editing the business policy.
dependency-inversion.meaning: High-level policy and low-level details should cooperate through abstractions. The abstraction expresses what the policy needs; concrete implementations decide how to provide it.
dependency-inversion.why: Notification implementations can be replaced during assembly. Order behavior can be tested without actually sending email.
dependency-inversion.beforeNote: The policy selects and creates a concrete email implementation.
dependency-inversion.afterNote: The policy depends on Notifier and receives its implementation. Injection is a mechanism; the dependency boundary is the goal.
dependency-inversion.when: Database, network, or messaging details make business behavior hard to replace or expensive to test.
dependency-inversion.caution: Dependency inversion is not identical to dependency injection and does not require a container. Injecting a concrete class alone does not establish a good abstraction.
dependency-inversion.remember: Let technical details serve the policy's contract.
dependency-inversion.connection: Strategy, Bridge, and Abstract Factory can isolate implementations. Merely using one of these patterns does not guarantee a sound dependency direction.

composition-over-inheritance.name: Composition over Inheritance
composition-over-inheritance.summary: Combine capabilities instead of creating a subclass for every combination.
composition-over-inheritance.question: Why does caching plus signing need yet another report subclass?
composition-over-inheritance.scenario: Reports can be cached or signed, then need both. Modeling every combination through inheritance steadily multiplies subclasses.
composition-over-inheritance.meaning: Prefer reusing behavior through composition or aggregation. Hold collaborating objects and delegate to them, assembling capabilities as needed rather than fixing every combination in a hierarchy.
composition-over-inheritance.why: Caching and signing can be maintained and tested independently, then combined without creating every possible feature subclass.
composition-over-inheritance.beforeNote: Every feature combination tends to add another subclass.
composition-over-inheritance.afterNote: Signing and caching become composable wrappers around the same report contract.
composition-over-inheritance.when: Capabilities vary independently, hierarchies become deep, or combinations cause a rapid increase in subclasses.
composition-over-inheritance.caution: Inheritance is not forbidden. Stable substitutable type relationships can justify it. Composition also adds delegation and assembly costs.
composition-over-inheritance.remember: Compose reusable capabilities; inherit only a sound type relationship.
composition-over-inheritance.connection: Decorator composes wrappers directly; Strategy delegates to replaceable algorithms; Bridge combines two independent dimensions.

law-of-demeter.name: Law of Demeter
law-of-demeter.summary: Talk to direct collaborators without depending on their internal networks.
law-of-demeter.question: Why does reorganizing addresses break shipping code?
law-of-demeter.scenario: Shipping code reads customer.profile.address.city. It knows several internal layers, so restructuring the customer can affect distant callers.
law-of-demeter.meaning: Also called the principle of least knowledge. A module should know the necessary capabilities of its direct collaborators, rather than manipulating a chain of their internals.
law-of-demeter.why: Internal reorganizations have less impact on distant callers, knowledge dependencies shrink, and collaboration boundaries become clearer.
law-of-demeter.beforeNote: The caller depends on three internal object layers for a simple request.
law-of-demeter.afterNote: The caller needs the city capability of ShippingDestination. The implementation owns its internal organization.
law-of-demeter.when: Behavior repeatedly traverses internal object graphs, refactoring requires changing distant callers, or services know too much about one another.
law-of-demeter.caution: Do not mechanically ban every dot or wrap every field of a plain data record. Focus on unnecessary knowledge dependencies between behavior-bearing modules.
law-of-demeter.remember: Ask a collaborator for a capability, not its internal world.
law-of-demeter.connection: Facade offers task-oriented entry points; Mediator coordinates relationships. Neither should become an all-knowing object responsible for everything.
